name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,333

entries.clue: Shout about name for candle-maker (9)

annotation.definitionNote: Chandlery is the candle-maker's trade or wares, not the maker himself; 'for' points the answer at him.

indicatorNotes.about: the shout goes round, about, the name

blocks.note: to cry = to shout; it wraps round the next piece
a handle is a name, as in a nickname or username

annotation.surface: Someone yells out a name on behalf of a candle-maker, perhaps calling a customer.
annotation.walkthrough: A chandler made candles; chandlery is his trade and goods, so the definition is a little loose and 'for' carries it.
annotation.definitionFit: Chandlery is the business of a chandler, the old word for a candle-maker.

entries.clue: Hamper containing sheer garments (8)

indicatorNotes.containing: the clog holds the next word inside it

annotation.surface: A laundry hamper full of see-through garments.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hamper' reads as a laundry basket, which suits the garments perfectly; it is the verb, to obstruct.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: garments taken together make up what you wear.

entries.clue: Period drama getting remade at last (3)

indicatorNotes.at last: take the last letter of each of the words before it

blocks.note: the last letters of dramA gettinG remadE

annotation.surface: A costume drama is being remade at long last.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Period drama' is a fixed phrase, so 'Period' hides as an adjective; it is the definition, a noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as in the Stone Age or the Victorian period.

entries.clue: European wife (5)

blocks.note: London Cockney slang for a wife, short for 'duchess'

annotation.surface: A man's wife comes from somewhere in Europe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'My old dutch' is London Cockney slang for one's wife, probably short for 'duchess'.
annotation.definitionFit: Dutch means of the Netherlands, and in Cockney slang a man's dutch is his wife.

entries.clue: Grand exploits transformed supernova? (9,4)

indicatorNotes.transformed: the letters are changed into a new form

annotation.surface: Great feats turned into something as dramatic as a supernova.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as a description rather than a synonym: a supernova is one kind of exploding star.
annotation.definitionFit: A supernova is a star blowing itself apart in a vast explosion.

entries.clue: Where to watch videos of second person underground (7)

blocks.note: the Tube is London's underground railway

annotation.surface: Videos of someone else filmed on the underground.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second person' is grammar, not a second individual; the Tube is the popular name for London's Underground.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the video-sharing website is where people go to watch clips.

entries.clue: Cleaner ignoring Henry Ford? (3)

indicatorNotes.ignoring: leave out the letter named next

blocks.note: a char is a cleaning lady
H = henry, the unit of inductance; removed from CHAR

annotation.surface: A cleaner pays no attention to the carmaker Henry Ford.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Henry Ford' reads as the carmaker; the name splits, Henry giving H and Ford, with its question mark, being one example of a car.
annotation.definitionFit: A Ford is a make of car, so the question mark flags a definition by example.

entries.clue: Smoke elevated better magic after dropping introductions (9)

indicatorNotes.elevated: in a down answer, raised up means written bottom to top
indicatorNotes.after dropping introductions: each word first loses its opening letter

blocks.note: MAGIC without its first letter; with ETTER, the whole string then reads upward

annotation.surface: A smoke that lifts a magic act, once the preliminaries are done.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Elevated' sits beside 'Smoke' as if smoke were rising; it is the reversal instruction for this down answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as in 'nip out for a smoke'.

entries.clue: Scottish region seen in crossword (4)

indicatorNotes.seen in: the answer can be seen inside the next word

annotation.surface: A Scottish place name turns up in a crossword.
annotation.walkthrough: Ross is an area of the northern Scottish Highlands, as in the old county of Ross and Cromarty.
annotation.definitionFit: Ross is a historic region of northern Scotland.

entries.clue: Honest option includes having everything in the same place (3,4)

annotation.definition: having everything in the same place

indicatorNotes.includes: the phrase holds the answer inside it

annotation.surface: The honest choice is to keep everything together in one place.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the word break between 'Honest' and 'option'.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a shop of this kind sells everything a customer needs under one roof.

entries.clue: Strongly suggests Boost when cycling (5)

indicatorNotes.when cycling: move a letter from one end round to the other

blocks.note: a surge is a boost; its S cycles from front to back

annotation.surface: An advert strongly recommends a boost from a bike ride.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' looks like riding a bike; it is the instruction to rotate SURGE into URGES.
annotation.definitionFit: To urge is to press or strongly suggest.

entries.clue: Bitter potato dish includes last of pepper (5)

indicatorNotes.includes: the dish takes the letter inside it
indicatorNotes.last of: take only the final letter of the next word

blocks.note: hash is a fried dish of chopped potato

annotation.surface: A bitter-tasting potato dish, once the pepper goes in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bitter' seems to describe how the dish tastes; it is the definition, as in a bitter wind.
annotation.definitionFit: Harsh and bitter both describe something severe and unpleasant.

entries.clue: Routes around town: right one drags on, unfortunately (4,5)

indicatorNotes.unfortunately: things going wrong suggest the letters falling out of order

annotation.surface: A grumble that the right bypass round town seems to go on for ever.
annotation.walkthrough: The complaint about a road that drags on is apt, and hides that 'right one' supplies two letters to the mix.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: these roads encircle a town so traffic can bypass its centre.

entries.clue: Works of Einstein usually varied, relativity especially, at first (6)

indicatorNotes.at first: take the first letter of each word in the run

blocks.clueFragment: of Einstein usually varied, relativity especially
blocks.note: first letters of Of Einstein Usually Varied Relativity Especially

annotation.surface: A comment that Einstein's output was varied, with relativity foremost.
annotation.walkthrough: The run begins at 'of', which looks like it belongs with 'Works'; the definition is 'Works' alone.
annotation.definitionFit: An oeuvre is the whole body of an artist's or thinker's works.

entries.clue: Something from auction wrongly carried by FA ships (8)

indicatorNotes.carried by: the letters are held inside FA

blocks.note: the outer letters, taken as they are
a lot is an item sold at auction

annotation.surface: An auction item wrongly shipped by the Football Association.
annotation.walkthrough: FA looks like the Football Association, England's football body; here it is just the two letters F and A that hold LOT and ILL.
annotation.definitionFit: A collective noun: the word names a small fleet, a group of vessels.

entries.clue: Iceland cannot change as planned (13)

annotation.surface: Iceland is unable to alter its plans.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cannot change' reads as a political statement; 'change' is the anagram instruction on ICELAND CANNOT.
annotation.definitionFit: Something non-accidental happened as planned, on purpose.

entries.clue: Dance in Ireland? I would in Chile, alternatively (7)

indicatorNotes.in: the first piece goes inside the second
indicatorNotes.alternatively: the letters are arranged another way

blocks.note: anagram fodder, rearranged to wrap round ID

annotation.surface: Someone would pick a Chilean dance over an Irish one.
annotation.walkthrough: A ceilidh is a Gaelic social evening of folk dancing, in Scotland or Ireland; the question mark admits Ireland is only one home of it.
annotation.definitionFit: A ceilidh is a Scottish or Irish gathering with traditional dancing.

entries.clue: Difficult job for judge (6)

blocks.note: a judge hears court cases, putting defendants on trial

annotation.surface: Judging is a hard job.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one opinion about judges, but it splits after 'Difficult' into two separate meanings.
annotation.definitionFit: A trying situation is difficult, and trying a case is what a judge does.

entries.clue: Split Conservative and non-Conservative? (5)

blocks.note: the political left, opposed to the Conservatives

annotation.surface: A party torn between Conservatives and everyone else.
annotation.walkthrough: The Conservatives are Britain's (and Canada's) right-wing party, so 'non-Conservative' is the political left.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as in a cleft chin or a rock split by frost.

entries.clue: Company adopting communist principles (5)

indicatorNotes.adopting: the company takes the next word into itself

annotation.surface: A firm takes up communist ideals.
annotation.walkthrough: RED for a communist is a crossword staple, from the red flag.
annotation.definitionFit: Latin for 'I believe': a statement of the beliefs that guide someone.

entries.clue: Delight to hold English or Australian baby (4)

indicatorNotes.to hold: the word wraps around the next letter

annotation.surface: The pleasure of cuddling an English or an Australian infant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Australian baby' sounds like a human child; a joey is a baby kangaroo.
annotation.definitionFit: A joey is a young kangaroo or other marsupial, an Australian baby animal.

entries.clue: Arabic person breaking soil in the centre (5)

indicatorNotes.breaking: the person splits the other letters apart
indicatorNotes.in the centre: take the middle letters of the word before

blocks.note: the middle two letters of sOIl

annotation.surface: An Arab person digs up the middle of a field.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Arabic person' reads as one phrase, but the definition is 'Arabic' alone; 'person' begins the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: By example: Oman is an Arab country, so Omani is one Arabic nationality.

entries.clue: Protection for piggy thrown into ale (7)

indicatorNotes.thrown: the letters are tossed into a new order

annotation.surface: Something to protect a pig, tossed into a vat of beer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Piggy' is a toe, from the nursery rhyme 'This little piggy went to market'; 'into' is fodder, not a container instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A toenail covers and protects the toe, a 'piggy' in nursery talk.

entries.clue: Boxer involved in philanthropy after retiring (3)

indicatorNotes.involved in: the answer sits inside the next word
indicatorNotes.after retiring: retiring means going back, so read the letters backwards

blocks.note: three letters inside phILAnthropy, to be read backwards

annotation.surface: A boxer takes up charity work once he has retired.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface fits Muhammad Ali's later life, and 'retiring' seems to belong to it; it is the reversal instruction, turning ILA round.
annotation.definitionFit: Muhammad Ali was a world heavyweight boxing champion.

entries.clue: Viewers missing start? That’s right (3)

indicatorNotes.missing start: the word lacks its start, so its first letter is left off

blocks.note: eyes are what we view with; EYES without its E

annotation.surface: Did the audience miss the beginning? Yes, they did.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Viewers' reads as a TV audience; here it means eyes.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Yes' is what you say to confirm that something is right.

entries.clue: Confused monarch with AI instrument (9)

indicatorNotes.Confused: a confused mind gets things out of order, so the letters come out jumbled

annotation.surface: A bewildered king faced with an artificial-intelligence gadget.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With' here adds AI to MONARCH as fodder, so it is part of the wordplay rather than a link to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A harmonica is a mouth organ, a musical instrument.
